prompt.context: A company is considering entering into the pick-up truck market. An investment of 1 billion dollars is required to build a plant. Currently, 750,000 pick-up trucks are sold in this market.
prompt.question: Should the company enter the pick-up truck market?

clarifying_info.q: What is the current market price for pick-up trucks?

clarifying_info.a: The plant can produce 200,000 trucks per year

clarifying_info.q: What is the elasticity of demand in this market?
What is the variable cost per truck?
What is the cost of capital?

clarifying_info.a: The plant has a life of 10 years

clarifying_info.q: What happens to the $1B investment at the end?
clarifying_info.a: The $1 billion must be returned at the end of the plant life

exhibits.title: Market data for pick-up trucks
exhibits.shows: A table listing key market parameters and a demand curve diagram for pick-up trucks

framework: Step 1: Estimate the impact of market entry on price using demand elasticity
Step 2: Calculate the new equilibrium price after adding company volume to the market
Step 3: Assess profitability at the new price given variable cost, capacity, plant life, and cost of capital
Step 4: Conclude with a go/no-go recommendation and flag strategic considerations (e.g., competitive dynamics, Cournot equilibrium)

questions.prompt: If the company enters at full capacity (200K units), how will the market price change?
questions.guidance: Candidate should use the elasticity formula. The percentage change in quantity supplied = 200K/750K ≈ 27-30%. With elasticity = 3, %ΔP = %ΔQ / elasticity = 30%/3 = 10%. New price = 30K × (1 - 10%) = 27K.

math.setup: Elasticity of demand = %ΔQ / %ΔP. Solve for %ΔP = %ΔQ / elasticity.

questions.prompt: At the new price of $27K and a variable cost of $20K, is the investment profitable over the plant life?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate contribution margin per truck, annual contribution, total contribution over plant life, subtract capital charges (10% × $1B/year × 10 years = $1B total), and subtract the return of the $1B principal. Total profit = $14B - $1B (capital charge) - $1B (return of investment) = $12B.

math.setup: Contribution margin = selling price - variable cost. Annual contribution = margin × volume. Total contribution = annual × plant life. Net profit = total contribution - total capital charge - return of investment.
steps: Capital charge = 10% × $1B = $100M per year; total = $1B over 10 years
Return of initial investment = $1B at end of plant life
math.answer: Total profit over plant life = $12 billion. The investment is highly profitable.

questions.prompt: The interviewer asks about the Cournot equilibrium and whether it is surprising that Toyota had entered the truck market. How would you address this?
questions.guidance: In a Cournot duopoly, firms compete on quantity. The case shows that even with a price reduction from new entry, margins remain very healthy (contribution margin of $7K/truck, ~23% margin). This makes entry attractive. Toyota's entry into the truck market is not surprising given the large profitability potential even after accounting for price erosion from additional supply. Candidate should acknowledge the strategic interaction between incumbents and new entrants.

brainstorming.prompt: Beyond the profitability math, what other factors should the company consider before deciding to enter the pick-up truck market?

categories.name: Competitive dynamics
ideas: Incumbent retaliation (price war, capacity expansion)
Number and strength of existing players
Cournot vs. Bertrand competition implications
Likelihood of further new entrants after this company's entry

categories.name: Market and demand
ideas: Market growth trajectory (is 750K growing or shrinking?)
Segmentation (light-duty vs. heavy-duty, commercial vs. consumer)
Cyclicality of pick-up truck demand
Geographic concentration of demand

categories.name: Operational capabilities
ideas: Does the company have relevant manufacturing experience?
Supply chain readiness for automotive components
Ability to achieve quality standards required by the market
Time to ramp up production to full 200K capacity

categories.name: Financial and strategic fit
ideas: Does $1B investment fit within capital budget?
Opportunity cost vs. other investments
Strategic rationale beyond NPV (brand extension, adjacent market)
Exit options if market conditions deteriorate

categories.name: Regulatory and external factors
ideas: Emissions and fuel economy standards
Safety regulations
Trade tariffs on vehicles or components
Labor relations in automotive manufacturing

recommendation: Enter the pick-up truck market. The NPV analysis strongly supports entry: total profit of $12B over a 10-year plant life on a $1B investment represents exceptional returns.
The demand elasticity analysis shows that even absorbing the 10% price decline caused by adding 200K units, the contribution margin of $7K/truck remains healthy at approximately 23%.
risks: Price erosion could be worse than modeled if incumbents aggressively expand capacity or cut prices beyond the Cournot equilibrium prediction
Demand could soften (cyclical downturn, fuel price spike) reducing volumes below 200K
Capital costs could overrun the $1B estimate
Execution risk in building and ramping a new automotive manufacturing plant
next_steps: Conduct detailed competitive analysis of incumbent strategies and likely responses
Validate demand elasticity estimate with market research
Develop phased entry plan to manage ramp-up risk
Assess manufacturing site options and partnership possibilities to reduce capital exposure
